items.title: Bungie unvaulting Destiny 2 content was a studio-saving emergency decision, because Marathon updates were never going to be enough
items.summary: At the last possible moment, Bungie takes a surprising and vital first step to winning back player trust.
items.body: Over the past couple of months, my Destiny 2 Fireteam has given me a tour of the Destiny 2 content I missed when I hopped off the train following the pandemic. When you play all the dungeons back-to-back, it's a buffet of delights—a concentrated dose of amazing and frequently obtuse FPS level design that you simply can't find anywhere else. A reminder that Bungie, pre-layoffs, was the very best at what it did. And yet, no game has had more caveats in its lifespan. There was always an amazing experience inside Destiny 2 somewhere , but recommending it to any normal person was out of the question. The onboarding for rookies was rough. Hoovering up all the expansions and dungeons was pricey and confusing. And after the release of The Final Shape, Bungie pissed off its player base repeatedly until the game was no longer sustainable. At what point would you ever advise a new player to jump in? Still, none of those issues compared to the content vault, first introduced in 2020. items.title: Blizzard warns World of Warcraft: Forever players it will 'very aggressively' punish anyone who buys gold with real money
items.summary: Preserving the economy of the MMO is a top priority, the studio says.
items.body: A common early World of Warcraft experience was to stumble into a series of corpses lying on the ground that, when looked at from the right angle, spelled out a URL for a site where you can pay real money for in-game gold. Gold was scarce back then, which spawned an entire market for buying it instead of grinding for it. Even if you never touched one of those sites, it was impossible to not see ads online or splayed out in front of you in a popular city. Blizzard has taken a light touch in the past when it comes to punishing people who willingly violate the MMO's EULA with real-money trading (RMT), but promises that won't be the case for World of Warcraft: Forever. In a recent Q&A , senior game designer Josh Greenfield addressed concerns about guilds letting players bid on items with gold (known as "gold dragon kill points" or GDKP) and the risks of RMT in WoW: Forever. He emphasized that Blizzard will "very aggressively punish gold buyers," to prevent the in-game trading economy from getting out of hand. "Being frank, we've been probably too lenient on gold buyers and it's been a little bit easy to get around some of our actions before and we are taking it very seriously," Greenf…

items.title: 'All roads lead back to Arma'
items.summary: Without Arma, gaming would look a lot different right now.
items.body: The ArmA family tree (Image credit: Future) This TikTok from Biffmatic (recently reshared by Bohemia Interactive) reminded me just how different PC gaming would look today if not for Arma, the long-running milsim series that's still going strong. Pretty much everyone knows that DayZ, one of the important PC games of the previous decade, began as an Arma 2 mod . The idea of PvPvE survival—the kind where you never know if you can trust the fella running down the road—was brand new, and it was such a hit that Arma developer Bohemia teamed up with DayZ creator Dean Hall to make a standalone version. DayZ went on to inspire a vibrant survival genre that's also given us Rust, Ark, and countless others. Did you also know that PUBG—and the entire battle royale genre, for that matter—is another Arma offspring? Brendan "PlayerUnknown" Greene developed the first version of PUBG as a mod to Dean Hall's DayZ mod. It was genuinely a mod of a mod, which Greene soon ported over to Arma 3. That mod was simply called "PlayerUnknown's Battle Royale" . It was my first introduction to the mode, and remains the mode I played most in Arma 3. items.title: Rockstar asks modders to please take its games very seriously
items.summary: In mod guidelines published earlier this month, Rockstar tells modders to "respect our games."
items.body: What happened On September 10, Rockstar Games published new mod guidelines on its website, which it says are intended to "maintain a fun, creative, and welcoming place for players and content creators." The guidelines are seem primarily targeted at mods for the FiveM and RedM platforms, which Rockstar acquired —along with their developers—in 2023. Rockstar says mods must "respect our games": As part of its "right to set limits on how others can use our games and brand," the studio says mods can't expand or modify official storylines, missions, and characters, and can't combine settings and characters from different Rockstar franchises. Rockstar says modders can't incorporate other intellectual property or real-world likenesses, and forbids cheat menus or modifications that interfere with its official multiplayer and online services. Rockstar calls its official modding platforms "the exclusive licensed home for our community to monetize their mods," forbidding alternative monetization or commercialization of mods for its games. items.title: World of Warcraft: Forever players competing over enemies is 'extremely important' to the experience, Blizzard says: 'This is one of those things that we simply must hold the line on'
items.summary: Blizzard better have some clever solutions for launch day, then.
items.body: When the gates opened on the World of Warcraft: Forever beta, it was a free-for-all. Everyone fought to be the first to "tag" enemies with their attacks so they would count for their quests—a problem that is essentially obsolete in modern WoW. My memories of doing this in the real classic WoW came flooding back as I frantically tried to claim enemies before someone else did. But that old frustration also prompted old solutions: Whenever I came across a quest to kill seven wolves or whatever, I invited other players into my group so that everyone got credit. This, according to senior game designer Josh Greenfield on X , is exactly what Blizzard wants to see. Greenfield responded to a conversation about whether or not shared enemy kill credit should be a thing in WoW: Forever to say pretty firmly that it's not going to change. "This is one of those things that we simply must hold the line on," he wrote. "I think there are other things we can do to help alleviate some frustration here but shared tagging is not it." items.body: ماذا قال نجم الهلال السابق؟ تجاهل ناصر الشمراني، أسطورة نادي الهلال، فراس البريكان، مهاجم الأهلي، فيما يتعلق بمركز رأس الحربة الأساسي للمنتخب السعودي خلال مواجهة الكويت، المقرر إقامتها مساء الأربعاء، في أولى جولات كأس الخليج العربي. ويقع الأخضر في مجموعة تضم الكويت وعمان والعراق، ولكنه يمتلك مجموعة جيدة من اللاعبين، بقيادة البريكان والحمدان ومحمد العويس وغيرهم، في الوقت الذي يبحث فيه المدرب اليوناني جورجيوس دونيس عن التشكيل الأنسب لبدء مشوار البطولة. ويرى الشمراني، صاحب الخبرة الكبيرة في مركز المهاجم، أن عبدالله الحمدان يبدو الخيار الأكثر جاهزية في الوقت الحالي، وهو ما يجعله يستحق الحصول على فرصة قيادة الخط الأمامي منذ البداية أمام الكويت. وقال الشمراني في تصريحات عبر برنامج "دورينا غير": "من وجهة نظري لم يصل أي لاعب في مركز رأس الحربة لجاهزية عبدالله الحمدان، ويجب على دونيس إشراكه بشكل أساسي من بداية المباراة ضد الكويت". ويعني رأي الشمراني أن الحمدان، من وجهة نظره، يمتلك في الوقت الحالي الجاهزية التي يحتاجها المنتخب في مباراة الافتتاح، خصوصًا أن البداية القوية في البطولة قد تكون مهمة بالنسبة للأخضر، الذي يخوض المنافسات على أرضه وبين جماهيره. اقرأ أيضًا.. السعودية قبل خليجي 27.. العراق عقدة تاريخية والكويت وعُمان في المتناول كما أن اختيار الحمدان لا يعني بالضرورة التقليل من إمكانا…

items.body: Lego announced a city builder called Lego Skylines last month and we all collectively said: " Oh yeah, duh ." A landscape of colorful bricks snapping together into a metropolis from the godlike perspective we already view our real life Legos just makes sense. Hold on, what about the brand I affectionately refer to as "digital Legos"? Minecraft should by rights have spawned a city building spinoff by now. How were Lego and Mojang not competing over this category of PC players years ago? Minecraft as a city builder: It makes sense Templated structures like villages, temples, and fortresses are already a staple in vanilla Minecraft Villagers: we love to exploit 'em and give them jobs Minecraft players love to build, why not cities? items.title: Bungie un-cancels Destiny: Vaulted content is coming back as new leadership promises 'Destiny is foundational to our future'
items.summary: "We are not done with Destiny."
items.body: Bungie's new leadership duo laid out the "next chapter of Bungie" today in a blog post with an accompanying video. The big news is that Bungie has essentially uncanceled Destiny 2, or will at least go the lengths to finally undo its greatest mistake: vaulting a bunch of raids and multiple of its story campaigns. Funnily enough, that work has already begun on the community side with a mod project that makes vaulted content playable through an offline build of Destiny. I got off the Destiny train a long time ago, but its "downward spiral," as PCG's Lincoln Carpenter put it in May , was a series of unforced errors that really began with the widely-hated decision to "sunset" (delete) gigantic chunks of the game in the name of "dealing with bloat." I still remember when a friend told me that the Destiny 2 campaign, I thing I bought and enjoyed in 2017, was simply gone. The news comes just three months after a brutal round of layoffs that affected hundreds of Bungie devs, essentially disbanding the Destiny 2 team. Whether you're on a bike, in a car, or hoofing it on-foot, it takes a while to get from the city itself out to the northernmost boonies. Well, no more. Flights V is a mod that turns GTA 5's airports into, ah, airports. items.title: Oh good, the pervert's back
items.summary: And it brought its kids.
items.body: While I've been pleased to watch Capcom begin teasing out previews of the expanded monster roster we'll face in Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance, its returning Elder Dragons have left me with a persistent feeling that something's still missing—something utterly detestable and unsettlingly phallic. Thankfully, that hole in my life has been filled. That hasn't stopped AMD from innovating though; by leveraging 'tetrahedral cages' to help render a vast scene of greenery, researchers at the company say they've managed to cut the potential ray tracing memory usage by 98%. Typically, a scene of around 25,000 independently animated plants made of hundreds of thousands of triangles could hoover up 80 GB of GPU memory. Holger Gruen, a Fellow of AMD's Advanced Graphics Program, recently shared on GPUOpen that the team's tetrahedral cage demos only use "1.7 GB of BVH memory and approximately 3.3 ms for all BVH updates per frame" in comparison. This was supposed to be the first five-day event in TGS' 30-year run⁠—while I am not a superstitious man, God or karma or something may be trying to tell us that it's just supposed to be a four-day deal. items.title: Feel like a kid again when toy car game Obstacle Overdrive launches October 2
items.summary: Be careful or your car will tumble to the floor and wake your parents up.
items.body: If you were fortunate enough to have toy cars when you were a kid—or rad enough to buy them for yourself as an adult—you probably had fun driving them over absolutely everything in your room. Mine could climb walls, scramble over book mountains, and drift around VHS-case race tracks. We'll soon be able to relive those memories without tipping pencils all over the table when Obstacle Overdrive launches October 2, 2026. Developed and published by Arcane Ermine, Obstacle Overdrive lets you go off-road—because it's all in a '90s bedroom—and make miniature radio-controlled cars navigate wacky obstacle courses. In the trailer, we see trucks going over toy keyboards, shimmying around block boards, and trundling over mountains of soft plushy toys. items.summary: Boldly step into the mist and confront whatever horrors may emerge.
items.body: When I first heard about this card-based roguelike city builder, I was confused. Then I played a round. And another. And another. And another. And before I knew it far too much time had passed and I was absolutely hooked. That game is Toxic Frontier, and we just revealed it at the PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct. Toxic Frontier plays on a hexagonal grid that makes it feel a bit like Settlers of Catan, only I'm not screaming at my housemates because they won't accept my very reasonable trade offers. You draw cards such as villages, forests, sheep, mountains, lakes, and more, and try to find the synergies while expanding into the titular toxic wasteland. items.title: Solarpunk MMO Loftia is launching into early access November 3
items.summary: Live on your very own island in the sky.
items.body: How come the future in videogames is, more often than not, dark and gloomy? Where's the hope? Where's the optimism? It's all in Loftia, an MMO life sim with a delightfully cheery, eco-friendly aesthetic. And, as was just revealed at the PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct, you'll be able to get your hands on it November 3. For those of you not in the know, Loftia is an eco-optimism life sim MMO that's been in development for the last four years. You and other players inhabiting the world will each get your own floating island to call home, and you've got a bunch of sustainable ways to decorate and power your slice of sanctuary. items.summary: I am being devoured by my own contradictions already.
items.body: Heads up, hotshot: you are being dispatched to a hostile alien planet. You will have to overcome life-or-death challenges that test your wits, physicality, and raw luck. You may die. You will almost certainly be hurt. Also, the whole thing is being televised. How many friends would you like to take with you? If you answered three, you're in luck—Marked For Mayhem is a four-player dungeon crawler which just got a world premiere at the PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct, and I pretty much just gave you its elevator pitch in the opening paragraph. The aim of the game is to venture to planets that would really quite like to kill you and complete bounties, beat foes, take on bosses, and even partake in a few minigames. items.body: Never say I'm biased or I don't have an open mind, because here I am, telling you about a videogame where raccoons—my favourite animal on this Earth—are the enemy. Heartbreaking, I know. In The Rabbit Haul, the crafty little scamps are pestering a bunny named Sprout, so they decide to turn their garden into a warzone that can keep the mischievous Trash Panda Posse at bay. Why does Sprout need to keep the raccoons away? Well, they kind of destroyed the town. I'm sure they didn't mean to and were just looking for snacks. Still, one has to defend one's home, so Sprout gets to planting deadly organic weaponry during the day and fighting off the hordes of ringtails at night. Sprout gets in on the action themselves, so you won't just be passively watching your plants do all the hard work. items.title: Core Keeper's Riders of the Underground update drops tomorrow, and you can get a sneak peek of it right here
items.summary: A new sub-biome, mounts, and more.
items.body: I can relate to the explorers in Core Keeper, because if I found an ancient, glowing orb, I know without a shadow of a doubt that I'd touch it, consequences be damned. Seems a lot of you feel the same way, because years after its early access release, Core Keeper is still going strong. We've just premiered a trailer for its new Riders of the Underground update, launching tomorrow, and it's a corker. The main addition, as the name of the update suggests, is rideable mounts. Every type of cattle can now be ridden into the depths. All you have to do is grab a saddle, a new item, and approach your desired mount. Once you've tamed your ride, you can change its name and decide on its behaviour—will it stay in place, follow you around, or roam aimlessly? You decide. items.title: Memory is the map in Wane, a roguelike where each biome is a corner of an archaeologist's fading mind
items.summary: An expedition unlike any other.
items.body: The best art is all about descending into someone's twisted psyche. It doesn't matter who, but the deeper we get into their very being, the better. Now buckle up and prepare for Wane, a roguelike where you quite literally navigate through the deconstructed mind of Declan Wayne, a fading archaeologist. We just revealed the game at the PC Gaming Show Tokyo Direct, and it looks like a corker—for any non-Brits, that means it looks really good.
